records.source: Ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν τῷ τὸν Ἀπολλῶ εἶναι ἐν Κορίνθῳ Παῦλον διελθόντα τὰ ἀνωτερικὰ μέρη ἐλθεῖν εἰς Ἔφεσον καὶ εὑρεῖν τινας μαθητάς, εἶπέν τε πρὸς αὐτούς· Εἰ πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐλάβετε πιστεύσαντες;
records.gloss: It came to pass now, while the Apollos was in Corinth, Paul, having passed through the upper parts, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples, \v 2 he said also to them, If [the] Spirit Holy did you receive having believed?
pieces: While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul made his way through the inland regions and came down to Ephesus. There he came upon some disciples
and asked them, "When you came to believe, did you receive the Holy Spirit?"

L.1: Now it happened, while Apollos was in Corinth, [that] Paul, having passed through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found some disciples,
L.2: and he said to them, "Did you receive [the] Holy Spirit when you believed?"

R.1: At that time Apollos was in the city of Corinth. Paul traveled through the high country inland and came to the city of Ephesus. He found some disciples there.
R.2: He asked them, "Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?"

decisions.choice: the upper regions: the higher inland country east of Ephesus
alternatives: a particular district called the Upper Parts
decisions.reason: Paul had set out through Galatia and Phrygia (18:23). The road from there to Ephesus came down from the high interior of Asia Minor to the coast.

decisions.choice: disciples: people who followed Jesus in some way, but knew only John's baptism
alternatives: full believers in Jesus who had already received the Spirit
disciples of John the Baptist, not of Jesus
decisions.reason: Luke calls the believers in Jesus "disciples" throughout Acts (6:1, 9:1), and Paul asks them about their believing. Yet they had not heard about the Holy Spirit and knew only John's baptism (19:2-3), like Apollos before Priscilla and Aquila taught him (18:25-26). How much they knew of Jesus is not said.

decisions.choice: when you believed: the receiving and the believing at the same time
alternatives: since you believed, at some time after it
decisions.reason: The participle and the main verb both look at a single past event, so Paul asks whether the Spirit came when they believed. The King James Version's "since ye believed" suggests a later, second event; the Greek does not.

decisions.choice: the city of Corinth; the city of Ephesus
decisions.reason: Readable says that the names are cities.

records.heading: Disciples who knew only John's baptism

records.source: οἱ δὲ πρὸς αὐτόν· Ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ εἰ πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἔστιν ἠκούσαμεν.
records.gloss: They and to him, But not even if [a] Spirit Holy there is did we hear.
pieces: They told him, "No. We never even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit."

L.2: And they [said] to him, "No, we have not even heard whether there is [a] Holy Spirit."

R.2: They answered, "No. We have never even heard that there is a Holy Spirit."

decisions.choice: whether there is a Holy Spirit: probably, whether the Holy Spirit has come and been given
alternatives: they had never heard of the Spirit at all
decisions.reason: John the Baptist spoke of one who would baptize with the Holy Spirit (Luke 3:16), so his followers would likely have heard of the Spirit. John 7:39 uses a similar short form, "the Spirit was not yet", meaning not yet given. Still, the words can be read plainly.

decisions.choice: but not even: a strong denial
alternatives: a contrast with what Paul said
decisions.reason: The words mean "no, not even": they had not received the Spirit, and had not even heard of such a thing.

decisions.choice: [said]
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves the verb of saying to be understood.

records.source: εἶπέν τε· Εἰς τί οὖν ἐβαπτίσθητε;
records.gloss: He said then, Into what then were you baptized?
pieces: Paul asked, "Then into what were you baptized?"

L.3: And he said, "Into what then were you baptized?"

R.3: So Paul asked, "Then what kind of baptism did you receive?"

decisions.choice: baptized into what: to what or to whom their baptism joined them
decisions.reason: To be baptized "into" a name is to be made over to that person (19:5; 1 Corinthians 1:13, 10:2). Paul asks what their baptism meant.

decisions.choice: Paul
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker.

decisions.choice: what kind of baptism did you receive?
decisions.reason: Readable asks the question in plain words; the meaning note explains the idiom.

records.source: οἱ δὲ εἶπαν· Εἰς τὸ Ἰωάννου βάπτισμα.
records.gloss: They and said, Into the of John baptism.
pieces: "Into John's baptism," they answered.

R.3: They answered, "We received the baptism that John gave."

decisions.choice: John's baptism: the baptism John the Baptist preached, a sign of turning back to God
decisions.reason: Apollos, from Alexandria, also knew only John's baptism (18:25). John's baptism had spread beyond Judea, and these men may have received it from others who had heard John.

records.source: εἶπεν δὲ Παῦλος· Ἰωάννης ἐβάπτισεν βάπτισμα μετανοίας, τῷ λαῷ λέγων εἰς τὸν ἐρχόμενον μετ’ αὐτὸν ἵνα πιστεύσωσιν, τοῦτ’ ἔστιν εἰς τὸν Ἰησοῦν.
records.gloss: Said then Paul, John baptized a baptism of repentance, to the people saying in the [one] coming after him that they should believe, that is in the Jesus.
pieces: Paul said, "The baptism John performed marked people's repentance, and he told the people to believe in the one who would come after him, namely Jesus."

L.4: And Paul said, "John baptized [with] a baptism of repentance, telling the people that they should believe in the one coming after him, that is, in Jesus."

R.4: Paul said, "John baptized people who were turning away from their sins and back to God. He told them to believe in someone who would come after him. That person is Jesus."

decisions.choice: a baptism of repentance: a baptism that showed people were turning from their sins to God
alternatives: a baptism that itself brought about repentance
decisions.reason: Luke 3:3 describes John's preaching in the same words. Repentance is a change of mind and life, turning back to God.

decisions.choice: the one coming after him: put first, for weight
decisions.reason: The Greek puts "in the one coming after him" before "that they should believe". Paul's stress falls on the one John pointed to.

decisions.choice: that is, Jesus: Paul names Jesus as the one John promised
alternatives: Paul adds a new teacher to John's message
decisions.reason: John said one more powerful than he was coming (Luke 3:16). Paul makes the same point in Pisidian Antioch (13:24-25): John's baptism looked forward to Jesus.

decisions.choice: people who were turning away from their sins and back to God
decisions.reason: Readable says what repentance means, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: ἀκούσαντες δὲ ἐβαπτίσθησαν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ·
records.gloss: Having heard then they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.
pieces: When they heard this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.

L.5: And having heard [this], they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.

R.5: When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Now they belonged to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: into the name of the Lord Jesus: made over to him, as his own
alternatives: a set form of words only
decisions.reason: As in 8:16 and 1 Corinthians 1:13, to be baptized into someone's name is to come under that person and belong to him. Compare "in the name of Jesus" in 2:38 and 10:48.

decisions.choice: Luke's words about the twelve men, not the end of Paul's speech
alternatives: still Paul speaking: those who heard John were baptized into Jesus
decisions.reason: Verse 6 goes on to tell how Paul laid his hands on "them", the same men, and nowhere is anyone said to have been baptized into Jesus's name by John. So the baptism here is a new one, given because John's baptism looked forward to Jesus.

decisions.choice: Now they belonged to him.
decisions.reason: Readable says what being baptized into his name meant, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: καὶ ἐπιθέντος αὐτοῖς τοῦ Παύλου χεῖρας ἦλθε τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐπ’ αὐτούς, ἐλάλουν τε γλώσσαις καὶ ἐπροφήτευον.
records.gloss: And having laid on them the Paul hands came the Spirit the Holy upon them, they were speaking then in tongues and prophesying.
pieces: Then as Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them. They began speaking in tongues and prophesying.

L.6: And when Paul had laid [his] hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they were speaking in tongues and prophesying.

R.6: Paul put his hands on them, and the Holy Spirit came on them. They began to speak in languages they had never learned, and they spoke messages from God.

decisions.choice: laying on of hands: a sign of prayer and blessing, here as the Spirit was given
decisions.reason: In Samaria the Spirit came when Peter and John laid their hands on the believers (8:17). Ananias laid hands on Saul for him to be filled with the Spirit (9:17).

decisions.choice: tongues: languages, as at Pentecost and in Cornelius's house
decisions.reason: The word means tongues or languages. At Pentecost the languages were understood by people from many nations (2:4-11); in Cornelius's house (10:46) and here, Luke does not say whether anyone understood them.

decisions.choice: prophesying: speaking a message given by God
decisions.reason: As Joel had said, those who receive the Spirit prophesy (2:17-18).

decisions.choice: speak in languages they had never learned; spoke messages from God
decisions.reason: Readable explains both words, as the meaning notes do.

records.source: ἦσαν δὲ οἱ πάντες ἄνδρες ὡσεὶ δώδεκα.
records.gloss: Were then the all men about twelve.
pieces: In all, the men numbered about twelve.

L.7: Now the men were about twelve in all.

R.7: There were about twelve men in the group.

decisions.choice: about twelve: a round number
alternatives: exactly twelve, a sign pointing to the Twelve apostles
decisions.reason: Luke uses "about" with numbers often (2:41, 4:4). He gives no hint that the number is a symbol.

decisions.choice: men: adult males
decisions.reason: The word means men; Luke counts the men of the group.

records.source: Εἰσελθὼν δὲ εἰς τὴν συναγωγὴν ἐπαρρησιάζετο ἐπὶ μῆνας τρεῖς διαλεγόμενος καὶ πείθων περὶ τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: Having entered then into the synagogue he was speaking boldly for months three, reasoning and persuading concerning the kingdom of the God.
pieces: Paul went into the synagogue, and for three months he spoke there without fear, debating and trying to win people over about the kingdom of God.

L.8: And having entered into the synagogue, he spoke boldly for three months, reasoning and persuading concerning the kingdom of God.

R.8: For three months Paul went to the synagogue and spoke there without fear. He discussed the Scriptures with the people and tried to convince them about the kingdom of God, God's rule as king.

decisions.choice: the synagogue: the Jewish meeting place in Ephesus, where Paul had promised to return
decisions.reason: On his first short visit Paul reasoned in this synagogue, and its people asked him to stay longer; he left promising to come back if God willed (18:19-21).

decisions.choice: reasoning: discussing and arguing, from the Scriptures
alternatives: giving a lecture with no exchange
decisions.reason: The same verb is used of Paul in Thessalonica, where he reasoned from the Scriptures (17:2), and in Corinth (18:4). It means talking things through with others.

decisions.choice: persuading: trying to persuade
decisions.reason: The present participle describes an effort that went on. Verse 9 shows that not everyone was persuaded.

decisions.choice: the kingdom of God: God's rule, which comes through Jesus
decisions.reason: Jesus spoke of the kingdom of God after he rose (1:3), and Acts ends with Paul proclaiming it (28:23, 28:31). It sums up the message about Jesus.

decisions.choice: discussed the Scriptures; God's rule as king
decisions.reason: Readable says what Paul discussed and what the kingdom of God means, as the meaning notes explain.

records.heading: Two years in the hall of Tyrannus

records.source: ὡς δέ τινες ἐσκληρύνοντο καὶ ἠπείθουν κακολογοῦντες τὴν ὁδὸν ἐνώπιον τοῦ πλήθους, ἀποστὰς ἀπ’ αὐτῶν ἀφώρισεν τοὺς μαθητάς, καθ’ ἡμέραν διαλεγόμενος ἐν τῇ σχολῇ Τυράννου.
records.gloss: When however some were hardened and were disobeying, speaking evil of the Way before the multitude, having departed from them he took separately the disciples, every day reasoning in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.
pieces: Some, though, hardened themselves and refused to be persuaded, and they spoke against the Way in front of the gathering. Paul then withdrew from them, taking the disciples apart with him, and each day he held discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.

L.9: But when some were being hardened and were disobeying, speaking evil of the Way before the crowd, he withdrew from them and took the disciples apart, reasoning daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.

R.9: But some of the Jews there became stubborn. They refused to accept the message, and in front of everyone they said bad things about the Way, which is what the movement of Jesus's followers was called. So Paul stopped going to the synagogue. He took the disciples with him, and every day he taught and talked with people in the lecture hall of a man named Tyrannus.

decisions.choice: were hardened and disobeying: they set themselves against the message and refused it
alternatives: God hardened them against their will
decisions.reason: The first verb describes a growing stubbornness. The second means to refuse to be persuaded, and so to disobey; it is used of the Jews in Iconium who refused the message (14:2).

decisions.choice: the Way: the name for the movement of Jesus's followers
alternatives: a way of life in general
decisions.reason: Acts uses "the Way" as a name for the believers and their teaching (9:2, 19:23, 22:4, 24:14, 24:22). Apollos had been taught "the way of the Lord" (18:25-26).

decisions.choice: took the disciples apart: led the believers away from the synagogue to meet on their own
decisions.reason: The verb means to set apart. Paul withdrew, and the disciples went with him, as in Corinth (18:7).

decisions.choice: the lecture hall of Tyrannus: a hall used for teaching, known by the name of its owner or of a teacher who taught there
alternatives: a school Tyrannus ran for Paul
decisions.reason: The word first meant leisure, then a place where lectures were given. Nothing more is known of Tyrannus.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus"
alternatives: some manuscripts add "from the fifth hour to the tenth"
decisions.reason: Codex Bezae and some other Western witnesses add that Paul taught "from the fifth hour to the tenth", that is, from about eleven in the morning to four in the afternoon, the hot part of the day when the hall would be free. The addition is not in the main early manuscripts. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: some of the Jews there; which is what the movement of Jesus's followers was called
decisions.reason: Readable says who "some" were (the people of the synagogue, 19:8) and what "the Way" was, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: stopped going to the synagogue
decisions.reason: Readable says what withdrawing from them meant.

records.source: τοῦτο δὲ ἐγένετο ἐπὶ ἔτη δύο, ὥστε πάντας τοὺς κατοικοῦντας τὴν Ἀσίαν ἀκοῦσαι τὸν λόγον τοῦ κυρίου, Ἰουδαίους τε καὶ Ἕλληνας.
records.gloss: This then continued for years two, so that all those inhabiting the Asia heard the word of the Lord, Jews both and Greeks.
pieces: This carried on for two years, with the result that all the people of the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord.

L.10: And this continued for two years, so that all who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.

R.10: Paul kept doing this for two years. Because of this, all the people who lived in the province of Asia heard the word of the Lord. Jews heard it, and Greeks heard it too.

decisions.choice: Asia: the Roman province in the west of Asia Minor, with Ephesus as its leading city
decisions.reason: Asia in the New Testament is the Roman province. Ephesus was its greatest city and the seat of its governor.

decisions.choice: all who lived in Asia heard: a sweeping way of saying the message reached the whole province
decisions.reason: Others carried the message out from Ephesus. Churches at Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis knew Paul's fellow worker Epaphras rather than Paul himself (Colossians 1:7, 2:1, 4:13).

decisions.choice: Greeks: non-Jews, people of Greek speech and culture
decisions.reason: Set beside "Jews", the word stands for the Gentiles of the province (compare 14:1, 18:4).

decisions.choice: the province of Asia
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say that Asia is a province, not the continent.

records.source: Δυνάμεις τε οὐ τὰς τυχούσας ὁ θεὸς ἐποίει διὰ τῶν χειρῶν Παύλου, ὥστε καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀσθενοῦντας ἀποφέρεσθαι ἀπὸ τοῦ χρωτὸς αὐτοῦ σουδάρια ἢ σιμικίνθια καὶ ἀπαλλάσσεσθαι ἀπ’ αὐτῶν τὰς νόσους, τά τε πνεύματα τὰ πονηρὰ ἐκπορεύεσθαι.
records.gloss: Miracles then not the ordinary the God was doing through the hands of Paul, \v 12 so that even to the ailing were carried away from the skin of him handkerchiefs or aprons and departed from them the diseases, the and spirits the evil went out.
pieces: God worked miracles of no common kind through Paul's hands,
so that people would even take cloths and work aprons that had touched his skin to those who were ill. Their sicknesses left them, and the evil spirits came out.

L.11: And God was doing not-ordinary miracles through the hands of Paul,
L.12: so that even handkerchiefs or aprons [that had touched] his skin were carried away to the sick, and the diseases left them, and the evil spirits went out.

R.11: God used Paul to do miracles that were very unusual.
R.12: People even took small cloths and aprons that had touched Paul's skin, and they carried them to sick people. Then the sicknesses left them, and evil spirits came out of them.

decisions.choice: not ordinary: unusual, extraordinary
decisions.reason: "Not the ones that happen by chance" is a way of saying "remarkable", with the stress on how unusual they were (compare 28:2).

decisions.choice: God did the miracles, through Paul
alternatives: the power belonged to Paul or to the cloths
decisions.reason: God is the subject of the verb. The story that follows (19:13-19) sets this beside magic, in which people tried to use a name as a spell.

decisions.choice: handkerchiefs and aprons: cloths for wiping sweat, and the aprons of a working man
decisions.reason: Both are Latin words taken into Greek. The first is a cloth for the face or for wrapping (Luke 19:20, John 11:44). The second is an apron or half-belt worn at work, fitting for Paul, who worked with his hands in Ephesus (20:34; compare 18:3). Exactly which cloths are meant is not certain.

decisions.choice: the diseases and the evil spirits: both healing and freeing from spirits
decisions.reason: Luke, like the Gospels, tells of sickness and of evil spirits as two kinds of trouble (Luke 6:18, 7:21).

decisions.choice: that had touched his skin
decisions.reason: "From his skin" means cloths that had been on his body; every level supplies the verb, Literal in brackets.

records.heading: The sons of Sceva and the books of magic

records.source: ἐπεχείρησαν δέ τινες καὶ τῶν περιερχομένων Ἰουδαίων ἐξορκιστῶν ὀνομάζειν ἐπὶ τοὺς ἔχοντας τὰ πνεύματα τὰ πονηρὰ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ λέγοντες· Ὁρκίζω ὑμᾶς τὸν Ἰησοῦν ὃν Παῦλος κηρύσσει.
records.gloss: Attempted now some also of the itinerant Jews exorcists to name over those having the spirits the evil the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, I adjure you [by] the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.
pieces: There were also some Jewish exorcists who traveled from town to town, and they tried calling on the name of the Lord Jesus over people who had evil spirits. "I charge you by the Jesus whom Paul preaches," they would say.

L.13: Now some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists also attempted to name the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had the evil spirits, saying, "I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims."

R.13: Some Jews traveled from town to town and tried to force evil spirits out of people. Some of these men also tried to use the name of the Lord Jesus to do it. They said to the evil spirits, "By the power of Jesus, the one Paul preaches about, I order you to come out!"

decisions.choice: itinerant exorcists: people who went from place to place driving out spirits with spells and oaths
decisions.reason: Such exorcists were known among Jews and others. Josephus tells of a Jew named Eleazar who drove out demons with spells said to come from Solomon (Antiquities 8.46-48).

decisions.choice: to name the name over them: to use Jesus's name as a spell, without faith in him
decisions.reason: They speak of "the Jesus whom Paul proclaims", not of their own Lord. Luke shows that the name is not a magic word (compare 3:16, 8:18-24).

decisions.choice: I adjure you: I put you under oath, I command you by a higher power
decisions.reason: The verb means to bind someone by an oath. The man with a legion of spirits uses it to Jesus (Mark 5:7).

decisions.choice: I order you to come out!
decisions.reason: Readable says what the exorcists commanded; the meaning note explains the verb.

records.source: ἦσαν δέ τινος Σκευᾶ Ἰουδαίου ἀρχιερέως ἑπτὰ υἱοὶ τοῦτο ποιοῦντες.
records.gloss: Were now of a certain Sceva, a Jew, a high priest, seven sons this doing.
pieces: A Jewish high priest named Sceva had seven sons who were doing this.

L.14: Now seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish high priest, were doing this.

R.14: Seven sons of a man named Sceva were doing this. Sceva was a Jew who was called a high priest.

decisions.choice: a Jewish high priest: no high priest named Sceva is known
alternatives: a member of one of the chief-priestly families
a title Sceva or his sons claimed for themselves
decisions.reason: Josephus names the high priests of this period, and Sceva is not among them. In Acts the plural of the word also means the chief priests, the leading priestly families (4:23, 5:24), so Sceva may have belonged to such a family. Or he may have called himself a high priest to impress people who sought exorcists. The text does not say which.

decisions.choice: a Jew who was called a high priest
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the title as Luke reports it without saying it was an office he held in Jerusalem, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: ἀποκριθὲν δὲ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ πονηρὸν εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Τὸν Ἰησοῦν γινώσκω καὶ τὸν Παῦλον ἐπίσταμαι, ὑμεῖς δὲ τίνες ἐστέ;
records.gloss: Answering however the spirit the evil said to them, The Jesus I know and the Paul I am acquainted with, you however who are you?
pieces: The evil spirit answered them, "I know Jesus, and I am acquainted with Paul. But you, who are you?"

L.15: But the evil spirit answered and said to them, "Jesus I know, and Paul I am acquainted with, but you, who are you?"

R.15: But the evil spirit said to them, "I know who Jesus is, and I know about Paul. But who are you?"

decisions.choice: two verbs for knowing: to know Jesus, and to know about Paul
alternatives: the two verbs mean the same
decisions.reason: The spirit uses two different verbs. The first may point to knowing Jesus and his power, the second to knowing who Paul is. They may also be only a change of word.

decisions.choice: but you: stressed; they have no authority over the spirit
decisions.reason: The pronoun is set first for contrast. Jesus and Paul have authority; these men do not.

records.source: καὶ ἐφαλόμενος ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐπ’ αὐτοὺς ἐν ᾧ ἦν τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ πονηρὸν κατακυριεύσας ἀμφοτέρων ἴσχυσεν κατ’ αὐτῶν, ὥστε γυμνοὺς καὶ τετραυματισμένους ἐκφυγεῖν ἐκ τοῦ οἴκου ἐκείνου.
records.gloss: And having leapt the man on them, in whom was the spirit the evil, having overpowered both he prevailed against them, so that naked and wounded they fled out of the house that.
pieces: Then the man who had the evil spirit threw himself on them. He mastered every one of them and was too strong for them, so that they fled from that house stripped of their clothes and covered with wounds.

L.16: And the man in whom the evil spirit was leapt on them, and overpowering them all he prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.

R.16: Then the man with the evil spirit jumped on them. He was too strong for all of them and beat them. They ran out of the house hurt, with their clothes torn off.

decisions.choice: all of them
alternatives: both of them: only two of the sons were there
decisions.reason: The word usually means "both", but in later Greek it can mean "all", and verse 14 speaks of seven sons. Some think that only two of the sons were there that day.

decisions.choice: naked: stripped, perhaps of their outer clothes
decisions.reason: The word can mean without one's outer garment (John 21:7). Either way, they fled in shame.

decisions.choice: overpowered them and prevailed against them: the spirit was far too strong for them
decisions.reason: The two verbs say the same thing twice, for force.

decisions.choice: with their clothes torn off
decisions.reason: Readable says what being stripped means here, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: τοῦτο δὲ ἐγένετο γνωστὸν πᾶσιν Ἰουδαίοις τε καὶ Ἕλλησιν τοῖς κατοικοῦσιν τὴν Ἔφεσον, καὶ ἐπέπεσεν φόβος ἐπὶ πάντας αὐτούς, καὶ ἐμεγαλύνετο τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ.
records.gloss: This now became known to all Jews both and Greeks those inhabiting the Ephesus, and fell fear upon all them, and was being magnified the name of the Lord Jesus.
pieces: Everyone in Ephesus, Jews and Greeks alike, came to hear of this. Fear took hold of them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was more and more honored.

L.17: And this became known to all, both Jews and Greeks, who lived in Ephesus, and fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was being magnified.

R.17: All the Jews and Greeks who lived in Ephesus heard about this. They were all afraid, and they gave great honor to the Lord Jesus.

decisions.choice: fear fell upon them: a sudden awe at God's power
alternatives: fear of the man with the spirit
decisions.reason: Luke uses the same words when God acts in power (5:5, 5:11; Luke 1:65).

decisions.choice: the name was magnified: the Lord Jesus himself was praised and honored
alternatives: the name became famous as a charm
decisions.reason: The name stands for the person (3:16). The verb means to make great, to praise (10:46).

decisions.choice: was being magnified: went on being honored
decisions.reason: The imperfect describes something that continued.

decisions.choice: gave great honor to the Lord Jesus
alternatives: the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified
decisions.reason: Readable says what honoring his name meant, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: πολλοί τε τῶν πεπιστευκότων ἤρχοντο ἐξομολογούμενοι καὶ ἀναγγέλλοντες τὰς πράξεις αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: Many then of those having believed were coming, confessing and declaring the deeds of them.
pieces: Many who had believed began coming forward to confess and to disclose their practices.

L.18: And many of those who had believed came, confessing and declaring their practices.

R.18: Many people who had believed in Jesus came and admitted the wrong things they had done. They told everyone about them.

decisions.choice: those who had believed: people already believers
decisions.reason: The perfect participle describes people who had come to believe before this. Some of them had still not given up their old practices.

decisions.choice: practices: their deeds, here most likely their magic
decisions.reason: The word means deeds or practices. Verse 19 shows that the practices were magic.

decisions.choice: were coming: one after another
decisions.reason: The imperfect describes something that went on happening.

decisions.choice: the wrong things they had done
decisions.reason: Readable says that the practices were wrong, as verse 19 shows.

records.source: ἱκανοὶ δὲ τῶν τὰ περίεργα πραξάντων συνενέγκαντες τὰς βίβλους κατέκαιον ἐνώπιον πάντων· καὶ συνεψήφισαν τὰς τιμὰς αὐτῶν καὶ εὗρον ἀργυρίου μυριάδας πέντε.
records.gloss: Many now of those the magic arts having practiced, having brought together the books, were burning [them] before all; and they counted up the prices of them and found [it] of silver myriads five.
pieces: A good number of those who had practiced magic collected their books and burned them where everyone could see. When the value of the books was added up, it came to 50,000 silver coins.

L.19: And many of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned [them] before everyone; and they counted up their value and found [it to be] 50,000 [pieces] of silver.

R.19: Many of those who had used magic brought their magic books and burned them in front of everyone. They added up how much the books were worth. It came to 50,000 silver coins. That was a very large amount of money.

decisions.choice: magic arts: sorcery, the practice of magic
decisions.reason: The word means things done with too much curiosity, and so magic.

decisions.choice: the books: scrolls of spells
decisions.reason: Ephesus was famous for magic. Spells known as "Ephesian letters" were written and worn as charms.

decisions.choice: 50,000 pieces of silver: a huge sum, though its value today cannot be fixed
decisions.reason: The silver coin was most likely the drachma, about a day's pay for a laborer (compare the denarius in Matthew 20:2). So the books were worth something like the wages of 50,000 days of work. No modern equivalent is given, because the value cannot be known exactly.

decisions.choice: burned: kept burning them, one after another
decisions.reason: The imperfect pictures the burning going on.

decisions.choice: That was a very large amount of money.
decisions.reason: Readable says what the number meant, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: οὕτως κατὰ κράτος τοῦ κυρίου ὁ λόγος ηὔξανεν καὶ ἴσχυεν.
records.gloss: Thus with might of the Lord the word was growing and prevailing.
pieces: So with great power the word of the Lord kept growing and gaining strength.

L.20: Thus with might the word of the Lord was growing and prevailing.

R.20: In this way the word of the Lord kept spreading, and it showed its great power.

decisions.choice: "of the Lord" goes with "the word", and "with might" with the verbs
alternatives: by the might of the Lord, the word grew
decisions.reason: The Greek order allows either. Acts often speaks of "the word of the Lord" (19:10); "with might" is a fixed phrase meaning mightily.

decisions.choice: growing and prevailing: spreading, and overcoming what stood against it
decisions.reason: Luke says the word grew in 6:7 and 12:24. The second verb means to be strong, to win out; here over magic and the powers behind it.

records.source: Ὡς δὲ ἐπληρώθη ταῦτα, ἔθετο ὁ Παῦλος ἐν τῷ πνεύματι διελθὼν τὴν Μακεδονίαν καὶ Ἀχαΐαν πορεύεσθαι εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα, εἰπὼν ὅτι Μετὰ τὸ γενέσθαι με ἐκεῖ δεῖ με καὶ Ῥώμην ἰδεῖν.
records.gloss: After now were fulfilled these things, purposed the Paul in the Spirit, having passed through the Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, having said that, After the having been me there, it is necessary me also Rome to see.
pieces: After these events, Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go on to Jerusalem. "Once I have been there," he said, "I must see Rome as well."

L.21: Now after these things were fulfilled, Paul resolved in the Spirit, having passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying, "After I have been there, I must also see Rome."

R.21: After all this, the Spirit led Paul to decide to go to Jerusalem. On the way he would go through the provinces of Macedonia and Achaia. Paul said, "After I go to Jerusalem, I must go to Rome too."

decisions.choice: in the Spirit: guided by the Holy Spirit
alternatives: in his own spirit, that is, he made up his mind
decisions.reason: The phrase could be an idiom for making a firm decision (compare "put in the heart", 5:4). But Luke stresses that the Spirit directs Paul's journeys (16:6-7, 20:22-23), and the same phrase is used of Paul going "bound in the Spirit" in 20:22.

decisions.choice: must: it is necessary, as part of God's plan
decisions.reason: Luke uses this word for what God has planned (Luke 24:44, Acts 1:16). The Lord later tells Paul that he must testify in Rome (23:11).

decisions.choice: Macedonia and Achaia: the Roman provinces of northern and southern Greece
decisions.reason: Paul had founded churches there: in Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea in Macedonia (16-17), and in Corinth in Achaia (18).

decisions.choice: after these things were fulfilled: when this work was done
decisions.reason: The verb means completed. Luke marks the end of Paul's work in Ephesus.

decisions.choice: the provinces of
decisions.reason: Readable says that the names are provinces.

records.source: ἀποστείλας δὲ εἰς τὴν Μακεδονίαν δύο τῶν διακονούντων αὐτῷ, Τιμόθεον καὶ Ἔραστον, αὐτὸς ἐπέσχεν χρόνον εἰς τὴν Ἀσίαν.
records.gloss: Having sent then into the Macedonia two of those ministering to him, Timothy and Erastus, he remained a time in the Asia.
pieces: Paul sent Timothy and Erastus, two of the men who assisted him, on to Macedonia, but he remained in the province of Asia for some time longer.

L.22: And having sent into Macedonia two of those who ministered to him, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed for a time in Asia.

R.22: Paul sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia. But he stayed in the province of Asia a while longer.

decisions.choice: those who ministered to him: who assisted him in his work
decisions.reason: The verb means to serve or help. Timothy had worked with Paul since 16:1-3.

decisions.choice: Erastus: a helper of Paul, perhaps the Erastus of 2 Timothy 4:20
decisions.reason: The name was common. An Erastus stayed in Corinth (2 Timothy 4:20), and Paul sends greetings from Erastus, the city treasurer, in Romans 16:23. Whether any of them are the same man cannot be known.

decisions.choice: Timothy and Erastus, two of the men who assisted him
alternatives: two of those who assisted him, Timothy and Erastus
decisions.reason: Balanced names the two men first.

records.source: Ἐγένετο δὲ κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν ἐκεῖνον τάραχος οὐκ ὀλίγος περὶ τῆς ὁδοῦ.
records.gloss: Arose now at the time that a disturbance not small concerning the Way.
pieces: Around that time a serious uproar broke out over the Way.

L.23: Now about that time there arose no small disturbance concerning the Way.

R.23: About that time, there was a lot of trouble in Ephesus because of the Way.

decisions.choice: no small: very great
decisions.reason: Luke often says "no small" for something great (12:18, 15:2, 19:24).

decisions.choice: the Way: the movement of Jesus's followers
decisions.reason: As in 19:9, the believers and their message.

decisions.choice: in Ephesus
decisions.reason: Readable says where the trouble arose.

records.heading: Great is Artemis of the Ephesians

records.source: Δημήτριος γάρ τις ὀνόματι, ἀργυροκόπος, ποιῶν ναοὺς ἀργυροῦς Ἀρτέμιδος παρείχετο τοῖς τεχνίταις οὐκ ὀλίγην ἐργασίαν, οὓς συναθροίσας καὶ τοὺς περὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα ἐργάτας εἶπεν· Ἄνδρες, ἐπίστασθε ὅτι ἐκ ταύτης τῆς ἐργασίας ἡ εὐπορία ἡμῖν ἐστιν, καὶ θεωρεῖτε καὶ ἀκούετε ὅτι οὐ μόνον Ἐφέσου ἀλλὰ σχεδὸν πάσης τῆς Ἀσίας ὁ Παῦλος οὗτος πείσας μετέστησεν ἱκανὸν ὄχλον, λέγων ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶν θεοὶ οἱ διὰ χειρῶν γινόμενοι.
records.gloss: Demetrius for a certain by name, a silversmith, making shrines silver of Artemis, was bringing to the craftsmen no little business, \v 25 whom having gathered together and the in such things workmen he said, Men, you know that from this the business the wealth to us is, \v 26 and you see and hear that not only of Ephesus but almost of all the Asia the Paul this having persuaded has turned away a great crowd, saying that not are gods those through hands being made.
pieces: There was a silversmith named Demetrius who made silver shrines of Artemis, and he provided plenty of work for the craftsmen.
He gathered them, and the workers in trades like theirs, and told them, "Men, you know well that our wealth comes from this work.

You also see and hear what this Paul is doing. Not only in Ephesus, but across nearly the whole of Asia, he has won over a large crowd and drawn them away by telling them that anything made with hands is no god.

L.24: For a certain [man] named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, was bringing no little business to the craftsmen.
L.25: Having gathered these together, with the workmen in such [trades], he said, "Men, you know that from this business is our prosperity.
L.26: And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a large crowd, saying that those made with hands are not gods.

R.24: There was a man in Ephesus named Demetrius. He made small silver models of the shrine of the goddess Artemis, and his business gave a lot of work to other craftsmen.
R.25: Demetrius called a meeting of these craftsmen and others who did the same kind of work. He said to them, "Men, you know that we make a lot of money from this business.
R.26: But look at what this man Paul is doing! You can see it and hear it for yourselves. He has talked a great many people into turning away from our gods. He has done this here in Ephesus and in almost the whole province of Asia. He says that gods people make with their hands are not real gods.

decisions.choice: Artemis: the great goddess of Ephesus
decisions.reason: Artemis was the city's own goddess, honored in a huge temple counted among the wonders of the ancient world. She shared her name with the Greek goddess of hunting, but at Ephesus she was worshiped as a great mother goddess. The King James Version calls her by her Roman name, Diana.

decisions.choice: silver shrines: small models of the shrine or temple of Artemis, sold to worshipers
alternatives: silver offerings made for the temple
decisions.reason: The word means a temple or the inner shrine where a god's image stood. Small clay and marble shrines of Artemis are known, but none in silver has been found, so exactly what Demetrius made is not certain.

decisions.choice: Men: Demetrius speaks to the craftsmen and workmen of his trade
decisions.reason: The hearers are the workers of a trade that Demetrius has called together, and the address fits them as they were, so it is kept as it is.

decisions.choice: persuaded and turned away: won people over and drew them from the worship of the gods
alternatives: changed their minds on a small matter
decisions.reason: The second verb means to move someone from one place to another. Demetrius means that people stopped worshiping the gods of the city.

decisions.choice: gods made with hands are not gods: Paul's teaching about idols
decisions.reason: Paul said the same in Athens (17:24-29). Believers in Thessalonica had turned from idols to the living God (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

decisions.choice: small silver models of the shrine of the goddess Artemis
decisions.reason: Readable says what the shrines most likely were, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: we make a lot of money; turning away from our gods
alternatives: our wealth is from this business; turned away a large crowd
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what Demetrius means by wealth and what the people turned from, as the meaning notes explain.

records.source: οὐ μόνον δὲ τοῦτο κινδυνεύει ἡμῖν τὸ μέρος εἰς ἀπελεγμὸν ἐλθεῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ τῆς μεγάλης θεᾶς Ἀρτέμιδος ἱερὸν εἰς οὐθὲν λογισθῆναι, μέλλειν τε καὶ καθαιρεῖσθαι τῆς μεγαλειότητος αὐτῆς, ἣν ὅλη ἡ Ἀσία καὶ ἡ οἰκουμένη σέβεται.
records.gloss: Not only but this is endangered to us the part into disrepute to come, but also the of the great goddess Artemis temple for nothing to be reckoned, to be about also to be deposed of the majesty of her, whom all the Asia and the world worships.
pieces: It is not only that our trade risks being despised. The temple of the great goddess Artemis may come to count for nothing, and she, the goddess whom all Asia and the whole world worship, may soon be pulled down from her greatness."

L.27: And not only is there danger for us that this trade of ours will come into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing, and that she whom all Asia and the world worships is about to be brought down from her majesty."

R.27: There is a danger that people will stop respecting our business. But that is not all. People will also think that the temple of the great goddess Artemis is worth nothing. Everyone in Asia and in the whole world worships her. But soon she will not seem great anymore!"

decisions.choice: this part: our trade, our line of work
decisions.reason: The word means a part or share, and here the business that is theirs.

decisions.choice: the temple of the great goddess Artemis: her great temple outside Ephesus
decisions.reason: Her temple at Ephesus was counted among the seven wonders of the ancient world.

decisions.choice: all Asia and the world worship her: a proud boast
decisions.reason: Demetrius speaks with pride for his city. Her worship was indeed widespread around the Mediterranean, but he is stirring up his hearers.

decisions.choice: Demetrius moves from money to religion
decisions.reason: "Not only ... but also" sets the danger to their trade beside the danger to the goddess. The second sounds nobler, but it is joined to the first.

records.source: Ἀκούσαντες δὲ καὶ γενόμενοι πλήρεις θυμοῦ ἔκραζον λέγοντες· Μεγάλη ἡ Ἄρτεμις Ἐφεσίων.
records.gloss: Having heard then and having become full of rage they were crying out, saying, Great [is] the Artemis of Ephesians!
pieces: On hearing this they flew into a rage, and they kept shouting, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"

L.28: And when they heard [this] and were filled with rage, they cried out, saying, "Great [is] Artemis of [the] Ephesians!"

R.28: When the men heard this, they became very angry. They began to shout, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"

decisions.choice: Great is Artemis of the Ephesians: a cry of praise to the city's goddess
decisions.reason: "Great" was a title given to Artemis of Ephesus. The words were both worship and civic pride.

decisions.choice: they were crying out: they kept on shouting
decisions.reason: The imperfect describes a cry that went on and on, as in 19:34.

records.source: καὶ ἐπλήσθη ἡ πόλις τῆς συγχύσεως, ὥρμησάν τε ὁμοθυμαδὸν εἰς τὸ θέατρον συναρπάσαντες Γάϊον καὶ Ἀρίσταρχον Μακεδόνας, συνεκδήμους Παύλου.
records.gloss: And was filled the city with the confusion, they rushed and with one accord into the theater, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians, fellow travelers of Paul.
pieces: Confusion spread through the city, and with one impulse the people stormed into the theater, dragging along Gaius and Aristarchus, the Macedonians who traveled with Paul.

L.29: And the city was filled with confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theater, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians, Paul's traveling companions.

R.29: Soon the whole city was full of confusion. People grabbed Gaius and Aristarchus, two men from Macedonia who were traveling with Paul. Then the crowd all ran together into the theater.

decisions.choice: the theater: the city's great open-air theater, where public assemblies met
decisions.reason: The theater of Ephesus held about 24,000 people. Its ruins can still be seen. Cities used their theaters for meetings of the citizens.

decisions.choice: with one accord: all together, with one impulse
decisions.reason: The same word is used of the crowd that rushed at Stephen (7:57) and of the believers praying together (1:14).

decisions.choice: Gaius and Aristarchus: two of Paul's companions from Macedonia
decisions.reason: Aristarchus came from Thessalonica (20:4, 27:2) and was later with Paul in prison (Colossians 4:10). Gaius was a common name; the Gaius of Derbe in 20:4 may be another man.

decisions.choice: people grabbed Gaius and Aristarchus; then the crowd all ran into the theater
alternatives: they rushed into the theater, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus
decisions.reason: Readable tells the events one at a time.

records.source: Παύλου δὲ βουλομένου εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὸν δῆμον οὐκ εἴων αὐτὸν οἱ μαθηταί·
records.gloss: Of Paul however intending to go in to the people, not were allowing him the disciples.
pieces: Paul was ready to go in and face the assembled people, but the disciples kept him from doing so.

L.30: But when Paul wanted to go in to the people, the disciples would not allow him.

R.30: Paul wanted to go into the theater and speak to the crowd. But the followers of Jesus would not let him.

decisions.choice: the people: the citizens gathered as an assembly
decisions.reason: The word is used of a city's citizen body meeting together (12:22, 17:5).

decisions.choice: would not allow: kept him back
decisions.reason: The imperfect suggests they went on holding him back.

decisions.choice: go into the theater and speak to the crowd
decisions.reason: Readable says where Paul wanted to go and why.

decisions.choice: the followers of Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable says who the disciples were.

records.source: τινὲς δὲ καὶ τῶν Ἀσιαρχῶν, ὄντες αὐτῷ φίλοι, πέμψαντες πρὸς αὐτὸν παρεκάλουν μὴ δοῦναι ἑαυτὸν εἰς τὸ θέατρον.
records.gloss: Some then also of the Asiarchs, being to him friends, having sent to him were urging not to give himself into the theater.
pieces: Some of the Asiarchs, too, who were his friends, sent word to him and pleaded with him not to put himself at risk in the theater.

L.31: And some of the Asiarchs also, being his friends, sent to him and were urging [him] not to venture into the theater.

R.31: Some of the leading officials of the province were Paul's friends. They sent a message to him. They begged him not to go into the theater.

decisions.choice: Asiarchs: leading wealthy men of the province of Asia, who bore a title of honor
decisions.reason: The title appears in many inscriptions from Asia. Asiarchs were men of wealth and standing, linked with the provincial council and its festivals, but their exact duties are not certain.

decisions.choice: not to give himself into the theater: not to risk going in
decisions.reason: To give oneself into a place means to venture there, at one's own risk.

decisions.choice: being his friends: some of the city's leading men were friendly to Paul
decisions.reason: Luke shows that people of standing did not see Paul as a danger.

decisions.choice: the leading officials of the province
decisions.reason: Readable explains the title, as the meaning note does.

records.source: ἄλλοι μὲν οὖν ἄλλο τι ἔκραζον, ἦν γὰρ ἡ ἐκκλησία συγκεχυμένη, καὶ οἱ πλείους οὐκ ᾔδεισαν τίνος ἕνεκα συνεληλύθεισαν.
records.gloss: Others indeed therefore something other were crying out, was for the assembly confused, and the most not did know for what cause they had come together.
pieces: Meanwhile people shouted all kinds of things, some one thing and some another. The assembly was in chaos, and most of them had no idea what had brought them there.

L.32: So some were crying out one thing and some another, for the assembly was confused, and most did not know for what reason they had come together.

R.32: People were shouting different things. The whole assembly was confused. Most of them did not know the reason they had all gathered.

decisions.choice: assembly: the gathering of the people of the city, here a disorderly one
decisions.reason: The word is the ordinary Greek name for a city's assembly of citizens. Luke uses it of the believers (5:11) and of Israel in the desert (7:38); here it is the crowd in the theater, which the town clerk sets beside the lawful assembly (19:39).

decisions.choice: some one thing, some another: a babble of shouts
decisions.reason: Each shouted something different, as in 21:34.

decisions.choice: for: explains the shouting
decisions.reason: The crowd shouted different things because no one knew what was going on.

records.source: ἐκ δὲ τοῦ ὄχλου συνεβίβασαν Ἀλέξανδρον προβαλόντων αὐτὸν τῶν Ἰουδαίων, ὁ δὲ Ἀλέξανδρος κατασείσας τὴν χεῖρα ἤθελεν ἀπολογεῖσθαι τῷ δήμῳ.
records.gloss: Out of now the crowd they instructed Alexander, having put forward him the Jews; the and Alexander having motioned the hand was wanting to make a defense to the people.
pieces: Some of the crowd told Alexander what to say, since the Jews had pushed him forward, and Alexander signaled with his hand, intending to speak in his own defense to the people.

L.33: And some out of the crowd instructed Alexander, the Jews having put him forward; and Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the people.

R.33: The Jews pushed a man named Alexander to the front of the crowd, and some people told him what to say. Alexander raised his hand to get the people to be quiet. He wanted to speak to the crowd and defend himself.

decisions.choice: instructed: told him what to say
alternatives: concluded that Alexander was the cause
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to instruct, or to put things together and conclude. Some manuscripts have another verb meaning to bring forward, which the King James Version follows ("drew Alexander out"). Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Jews put him forward: probably to show that the Jews had no part in Paul's teaching
decisions.reason: Jews also refused to worship idols, and the crowd might blame them along with Paul. Luke does not say what Alexander meant to say. It is not certain that he is the Alexander of 1 Timothy 1:20 or 2 Timothy 4:14.

decisions.choice: motioned with his hand: a speaker's sign asking for silence
decisions.reason: Peter and Paul do the same before speaking (12:17, 13:16, 21:40).

decisions.choice: to get the people to be quiet
decisions.reason: Readable says what the gesture meant, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: ἐπιγνόντες δὲ ὅτι Ἰουδαῖός ἐστιν φωνὴ ἐγένετο μία ἐκ πάντων ὡς ἐπὶ ὥρας δύο κραζόντων· Μεγάλη ἡ Ἄρτεμις Ἐφεσίων.
records.gloss: Having recognized however that a Jew he is, a cry there was one from all, about for hours two crying out, Great [is] the Artemis of Ephesians!
pieces: But as soon as they realized he was a Jew, they all joined in one shout, and for about two hours they cried out, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"

L.34: But when they recognized that he was a Jew, one cry arose from them all, as for about two hours they cried out, "Great [is] Artemis of [the] Ephesians!"

R.34: But the crowd saw that Alexander was a Jew. So they all began to shout together, and they kept on shouting for about two hours, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"

decisions.choice: a Jew: one who would not worship Artemis
decisions.reason: Jews refused to worship idols, so the crowd took Alexander to be against their goddess too.

decisions.choice: the sentence changes its grammar part way: they recognized ... one cry from all
decisions.reason: The opening participle does not fit the rest of the sentence. The broken grammar suits the excited scene.

decisions.choice: the crowd; Alexander
decisions.reason: Readable names who saw whom.

records.source: καταστείλας δὲ ὁ γραμματεὺς τὸν ὄχλον φησίν· Ἄνδρες Ἐφέσιοι, τίς γάρ ἐστιν ἀνθρώπων ὃς οὐ γινώσκει τὴν Ἐφεσίων πόλιν νεωκόρον οὖσαν τῆς μεγάλης Ἀρτέμιδος καὶ τοῦ διοπετοῦς;
records.gloss: Having calmed then the town clerk the crowd says, Men Ephesians, who for is there of men who not knows the of Ephesians city temple keeper being of the great Artemis and of the fallen from heaven?
pieces: The town clerk managed to quiet the crowd and said, "{{gender:People|Men}} of Ephesus, is there anyone at all who does not know that this city of the Ephesians has been entrusted with the temple of the great Artemis and with the image that fell from heaven?

L.35: And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, "Men, Ephesians, who is there among {{gender:people|men}} who does not know that the city of [the] Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis and of the [image] fallen from heaven?

R.35: Finally the town clerk got the crowd to be quiet. He said, "People of Ephesus, everyone knows that our city takes care of the temple of the great goddess Artemis. Everyone knows that we also guard her image that fell from heaven.

decisions.choice: the town clerk: the city's leading official, who kept its records and dealt with the assembly
alternatives: a scribe who taught the law
a clerk who only wrote letters
decisions.reason: The word is the one used for the Jewish scribes, but in a Greek city it was the title of the chief official. Inscriptions from Ephesus show him drafting the assembly's decrees and acting for the city before the Roman authorities.

decisions.choice: Men of Ephesus: the formal address to the citizens, said here to a mixed crowd
decisions.reason: This was the usual way to address the citizen assembly. The crowd in the theater was a gathering of the city, likely men and women together.

decisions.choice: temple keeper: the city's title of honor as guardian of a temple
decisions.reason: The word first meant a temple warden. Inscriptions and coins of Ephesus use it as the city's proud title, guardian of Artemis's temple.

decisions.choice: the image fallen from heaven: a sacred object believed to have fallen from the sky
alternatives: the statue of Artemis made by human hands
decisions.reason: The Greek has only "the fallen from heaven" and leaves the noun to be understood. Most likely it was an image of Artemis believed to have come from the sky, perhaps a meteorite. The clerk answers the charge that gods made with hands are not gods (19:26): this one, he claims, no human hand made.

decisions.choice: people, with "men" as the alternative
decisions.reason: The word means human beings in general; Balanced and Readable use words that are already inclusive.

decisions.choice: People of Ephesus, with "Men of Ephesus" as the alternative
decisions.reason: As at 3:12, for a mixed crowd; the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: two plain statements
decisions.reason: Readable states what the clerk's question implies.

records.source: ἀναντιρρήτων οὖν ὄντων τούτων δέον ἐστὶν ὑμᾶς κατεσταλμένους ὑπάρχειν καὶ μηδὲν προπετὲς πράσσειν.
records.gloss: Undeniable therefore being these things, necessary it is you calm to be and nothing rash to do.
pieces: No one can dispute these facts, so you ought to keep calm and not do anything reckless.

L.36: Since these things are undeniable, then, it is necessary for you to be calm and to do nothing rash.

R.36: No one can say these things are not true. So you need to calm down. Do not do anything foolish without thinking.

decisions.choice: since these things cannot be denied: the clerk reasons from the city's honor
decisions.reason: His point is that Artemis's standing is secure, so there is no need for a riot.

decisions.choice: rash: reckless, done in haste
decisions.reason: The word means falling headlong, acting without thought.

records.source: ἠγάγετε γὰρ τοὺς ἄνδρας τούτους οὔτε ἱεροσύλους οὔτε βλασφημοῦντας τὴν θεὸν ἡμῶν.
records.gloss: You brought for the men these neither temple robbers nor blaspheming the goddess of us.
pieces: These men you have dragged here are not temple robbers, and they have not insulted our goddess.

L.37: For you have brought these men, [who are] neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.

R.37: You brought these men here, but they have not robbed any temple. They have not said bad things about our goddess either.

decisions.choice: temple robbers: people who steal from temples or commit sacrilege
decisions.reason: Paul uses the related verb in Romans 2:22. Robbing a temple was counted a grave crime.

decisions.choice: blaspheming our goddess: speaking insults against her
decisions.reason: Paul and his companions taught that idols are not gods (19:26), but they had not insulted Artemis.

decisions.choice: these men: Gaius and Aristarchus
decisions.reason: The crowd had dragged Gaius and Aristarchus into the theater (19:29).

records.source: εἰ μὲν οὖν Δημήτριος καὶ οἱ σὺν αὐτῷ τεχνῖται ἔχουσιν πρός τινα λόγον, ἀγοραῖοι ἄγονται καὶ ἀνθύπατοί εἰσιν, ἐγκαλείτωσαν ἀλλήλοις.
records.gloss: If indeed therefore Demetrius and the with him craftsmen have against anyone a matter, courts are held and proconsuls there are; let them bring charges against one another.
pieces: So if Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a case against anyone, there are court days and there are proconsuls; let the parties bring their charges against each other there.

L.38: So if Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a matter against anyone, court days are held and there are proconsuls; let them bring charges against one another.

R.38: Demetrius and the men who work with him may have a complaint against someone. If so, they should take it to the courts. The courts meet on certain days, and there are proconsuls, the Roman governors, to judge. There they can accuse each other.

decisions.choice: court days are held: the courts sit on set days
decisions.reason: The word describes days when the courts met, often in the marketplace.

decisions.choice: proconsuls: the Roman governors of the province
decisions.reason: Asia was governed by one proconsul at a time. The plural speaks of the office in general: there are such officials to hear cases.

decisions.choice: bring charges against one another: let the two sides go to law
alternatives: accuse each other of the riot
decisions.reason: The verb means to accuse in court. The clerk sends the dispute to the courts.

decisions.choice: the Roman governors, to judge
decisions.reason: Readable says who the proconsuls were, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: εἰ δέ τι περαιτέρω ἐπιζητεῖτε, ἐν τῇ ἐννόμῳ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἐπιλυθήσεται.
records.gloss: If however anything beyond this you seek, in the lawful assembly it will be settled.
pieces: Any further matter you raise will be dealt with in the lawful assembly.

L.39: But if you seek anything further, it will be settled in the lawful assembly.

R.39: If you want to deal with any other matter, it must be decided at a lawful meeting of the city assembly.

decisions.choice: the lawful assembly: the regular assembly of citizens, called according to law
decisions.reason: The clerk sets the lawful assembly beside the confused gathering in the theater (19:32). Public matters belonged to the citizens' assembly when it met in proper order.

decisions.choice: anything further: matters beyond a charge against a person
alternatives: any more charges against these men
decisions.reason: Charges against persons go to the courts (19:38); public questions go to the assembly.

records.source: καὶ γὰρ κινδυνεύομεν ἐγκαλεῖσθαι στάσεως περὶ τῆς σήμερον μηδενὸς αἰτίου ὑπάρχοντος περὶ οὗ οὐ δυνησόμεθα ἀποδοῦναι λόγον περὶ τῆς συστροφῆς ταύτης.
records.gloss: And for we are in danger of being accused of insurrection concerning the today, not one cause existing, concerning which not we will be able to give an account concerning the commotion this.
pieces: Indeed, today's events put us in danger of being accused of rebellion. There is no cause we could point to, nothing we could say to explain this disorderly gathering."

L.40: For indeed we are in danger of being accused of rioting over today's [events], there being no cause about which we will be able to give an account of this commotion."

R.40: We are in danger, because the Roman rulers could say that we started a riot today. There is no good reason for this crowd to be here. If they ask us about it, we will have nothing to say."

decisions.choice: insurrection: rioting, civil disorder
decisions.reason: The word means a rising or riot. Roman governors dealt harshly with cities that let crowds run riot, and a city could lose its privileges.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "about which we will not be able to give an account"
decisions.reason: With "not" the Greek has a double negative after "no cause", hard to put into words; without it the sentence reads more smoothly. Either way the sense is that they can give no reason for the gathering. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: commotion: a disorderly gathering, a mob
decisions.reason: The word means a crowd that has gathered together, here without lawful cause, set beside the lawful assembly (19:39).

decisions.choice: the Roman rulers could say
alternatives: we are in danger of being accused
decisions.reason: Readable names the likely accusers, whom the Greek leaves unnamed; the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: we will be able
decisions.reason: Literal leaves out the second negative of the Greek, which would reverse the sense in English; the meaning note explains.

records.source: καὶ ταῦτα εἰπὼν ἀπέλυσεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν.
records.gloss: And these things having said he dismissed the assembly.
pieces: With these words he sent the assembly away.

L.40: And having said these things, he dismissed the assembly.

R.40: After he said this, he told the assembly to go home.

decisions.choice: the assembly: the gathering in the theater
decisions.reason: The same word as in 19:32 and 19:39. The clerk treats the crowd as an assembly and closes it.

decisions.choice: told the assembly to go home
decisions.reason: Readable says what dismissing meant.
